title: The fourth truth
hookLine: the way that leads to the ending of dukkha: the eightfold path

cards: Three truths in, look at the verbs so far. Dukkha is to be understood. Craving is to be let go.
Its ending is to be realized. All three could, in principle, happen while sitting perfectly still. The fourth truth is different.
It's full of ordinary verbs: speaking, acting, earning a living, making an effort, paying attention. The first three say what's true. The fourth says where to put your feet on Monday morning.

teach.h: MAGGA: A ROAD THROUGH THE FOREST.
teach.b: The fourth truth is the way leading to the ending of dukkha. The Pali word is magga: a path, a road, a track through the forest. In the first sermon the Buddha names it: the noble eightfold path.
Right view. Right intention. Right speech.
Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort.
Right mindfulness. Right concentration. The word translated right is sammā.
Dictionaries also give it as properly or thoroughly, and some teachers render it complete or whole. Two things to notice. First, this path is the middle way.

The sermon begins by setting aside two extremes: chasing sense pleasure, and punishing the body. The eightfold path runs between them. Second, it's not a staircase where you finish step one before starting step two.

Some teachers compare it to the strands of a rope, or the spokes of a wheel, all working at once. Your speech affects your mindfulness; your mindfulness affects your view. You don't graduate from right speech.
And look how ordinary much of it is: three of the eight, speech, action and livelihood, happen at the kitchen table and at work, not on a cushion.

teach.h: STRANDS OF A ROPE, NOT STAIRS.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, names the path in its list of bests: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words."
Later in year two, we'll walk these eight one at a time.

how: Buddhists in many schools learn the noble eightfold path as the practical side of the teaching, and the eight-spoked wheel, a common Buddhist symbol, is often read as standing for it.

o: a path, a road to walk
a goal you reach at the very end
a list of rules to memorize

games.q: match each piece to the fourth truth.
p: worked like strands of a rope

s: the eight factors are steps you finish one at a time
teachers compare them to strands of a rope or spokes of a wheel, all working together.
the eightfold path is the middle way between two extremes
the first sermon sets aside sense-pleasure and self-punishment, and names the path between.
the eightfold path is only about meditation
speech, action and livelihood are on it too: much of it happens at work and at home.

games.q: you've just heard the first three truths: dukkha, its cause, its ending. what's the one thing still missing?
o: a list of who's to blame.
a promise of reward after death.
games.why: the fourth truth is the way: the noble eightfold path, which keeps the teaching from being diagnosis without treatment.

practice: Count the eight on your fingers, one per breath: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
Go around again, and with each one let a single picture from your own life come up: a conversation, a job, a moment of attention. If you lose your place, simply start the count again.

wordCard.voice: Magga. The path: the fourth noble truth, the noble eightfold path that leads to the ending of dukkha.

orig.note: Pali magga, Sanskrit mārga: a path or road; the fourth noble truth.

carryVoice: Your line: the path. Much of it already runs through an ordinary day. Until tomorrow.
